lesson.title: One Formula, Infinitely Many Curves
lesson.summary: The general antiderivative combines a specific antiderivative with the constant of integration into a single formula, F(x) + C, that represents the entire family of curves sharing a derivative.
lesson.body:
You now have the two pieces needed to name this idea precisely. The indefinite integral told you how to package all antiderivatives of a function into one expression, and the constant of integration told you exactly why that expression needs a floating C at the end. Put those two pieces together and you get the general antiderivative: the formula F(x) + C, where F is any specific antiderivative you found and C ranges over all real numbers.

The word 'general' is doing real work here. It distinguishes this formula from a 'particular' antiderivative, which is a single function picked out of the family, a distinction the next chapter will make precise. For now, the general antiderivative is the complete, unrestricted answer: it describes every function whose derivative matches the given integrand, all at once.

Let's build one from scratch. Suppose f(x) = 4x^3. We need a function whose derivative is 4x^3. Since d/dx[x^4] = 4x^(4-1) = 4x^3 by the power rule, x^4 is one antiderivative. The general antiderivative is then F(x) = x^4 + C. Verify by differentiating the general form directly: d/dx[x^4 + C] = 4x^3 + 0 = 4x^3, which matches f(x) regardless of what value C takes.

It helps to picture this general antiderivative graphically. If you plotted x^4 + C for many different values of C, say C = -2, 0, and 5, you would get a stack of curves, each one an exact vertical copy of the others, shifted up or down. At any fixed x-value, every curve in the stack has the identical slope, because they all share the derivative 4x^3. The general antiderivative is the algebraic description of that entire stack in one line, rather than an infinite list of separate equations.
